youtube.hook: How do casinos always win? Las Vegas Strip casinos kept $8.8 billion in 2025, about $1 million an hour. Here's the math and the tricks. Dave lands in Vegas with $500 and a plan: win. We explain the house edge on roulette (5.26%), blackjack and slots, how the law of large numbers turns a tiny edge into billions, the building's psychology tricks (no clocks, chips, free drinks, near misses, comps), and why sports betting apps grew 23% in a year.

beats.text: This is me last Friday walking into a Las Vegas casino with five hundred dollars and one plan which was to win.
Everybody online keeps posting giant piles of casino cash so how hard can it be right?
Spoiler.
By the end of this video you'll see exactly where my money went and the one trick the casino plays on you every single time you bet on anything.
And most people click off before that part which is exactly what the casino wants you to do.
So Friday night I walk in and it's bright lights and ringing bells and a carpet with a pattern that honestly looks like a migraine.
I'm a very smart person so I named my strategy the Dave Method. I couldn't think of anything else.
I swap two hundred dollars for these little plastic chips and I sit down at the roulette table like I own the place.
First spin I bet on red and it's red. Second spin I bet on red again and it's red again. I am clearly a genius.
Me after two spins.
One hour later I'm up one hundred and fifty dollars and I'm seriously thinking about quitting my job.
But here's the weird part. The casino isn't nervous at all. Nobody runs over to stop me and nobody even looks at me.
And that's because the casino knows something about that table that I didn't know yet.
So I looked it up and roulette was kind of invented by accident by a French genius named Blaise Pascal who was actually trying to build a machine that spins forever.
He failed and three hundred years later his failure is taking my money.
Here's the trick. If I bet on one number and it hits the casino pays me thirty five times my bet.
Sounds fair until you count the pockets because there are thirty eight of them and that sneaky green zero and double zero are the casino's little hiding spots.
Wait. Thirty eight?
So every time I play the wheel quietly keeps about five cents of every dollar I bet. It's not luck. It's a toll.
Five cents doesn't sound like much and that's exactly why it works on you.
It's like a tiny raccoon sitting inside every bet and taking a bite every single time you play.
So I said okay roulette is rigged so let me try a smarter game and I walked over to the blackjack table.
And blackjack actually is the best game in the building because in the sixties a math professor named Edward Thorp literally beat it with math.
He wrote a whole book about it and the casinos panicked so hard that they changed the rules and kicked people out.
Imagine being so good at math that a casino bans you.
But I'm not a math professor. I'm a guy who hit on sixteen because it felt lucky.
And then I saw the slot machines and they were beautiful and flashing and making happy noises at me.
Fun fact that I learned way too late. A slot machine can take a new bet every few seconds. That's hundreds of tiny tolls every hour.
My wallet watching me walk toward the slots.
Midnight check. I'm still up one hundred dollars. I feel unstoppable.
So why was the casino so calm while I was winning? Because the casino isn't playing my night. It's playing the average.
Flip a coin ten times and you might get seven heads and feel like a wizard.
Flip it a million times and it lands almost exactly half and half. The luck just melts away.
A Swiss mathematician named Jacob Bernoulli proved this more than three hundred years ago and casinos have been printing money with it ever since.
So me winning on Friday doesn't scare them at all. They don't need me to lose tonight. They just need me to keep playing.
And that sentence right there is the whole casino business in one line.
You're gambling. They're doing math. And math doesn't get tired.
Las Vegas casinos win about a million dollars every hour of every day and that's after paying every lucky winner like me.
The winners are real but they get paid with the losers' money and the house keeps its bite in the middle.
Quick guess before I tell you. What's the most money one person ever won in a row in Las Vegas? Think of a number.
His name was Archie Karas and in nineteen ninety two he walked into Las Vegas with fifty dollars.
Over the next three years he turned those fifty dollars into about forty million dollars. People call it the biggest winning streak in gambling history.
And then he kept playing.
In about three weeks he lost almost all of it. Forty million dollars gone because he didn't walk away.
That's the law of large numbers with a real face on it. Win big and the average still comes for you as long as you keep sitting at the table.
But math isn't even the creepiest part. The building itself is designed to keep you inside.
Look around a casino and try to find a clock or a window. You won't. No sun and no clock means you lose track of time and it's suddenly three in the morning.
Then there's the chips. Handing over a real hundred dollar bill hurts but tossing a little plastic chip feels like you're playing Monopoly.
And then they bring you free drinks which is very nice of them and also makes every bad bet look like a great idea.
Cheers to bad decisions.
And the slot machines do this evil little thing called the near miss where two jackpots line up and the third one stops just above the line.
Scientists at Cambridge scanned people's brains and found that a near miss lights up the same reward spots as a real win. Your brain literally thinks you almost won.
My brain at the slot machine.
Be honest. You've felt that. The claw machine that almost grabbed the toy. The scratch card that was one number off.
And the free hotel room and the free buffet? They're calculated from how much the casino expects you to lose. It's your own money coming back in a nicer outfit.
Enjoy the shrimp.
Back to my night. It's three in the morning. My lucky streak is gone and I'm down three hundred dollars and all I can think is I just need one big win to get it back.
And that thought right there is the most expensive thought in the whole building.
Because the next spin doesn't know I lost the last one. The wheel doesn't feel sorry for me. The toll stays exactly the same.
Me trying to win it back.
And the worst part is I don't even need to fly to Vegas to feel this anymore because the casino now lives in your pocket.
Since the Supreme Court opened the door in twenty eighteen sports betting is legal in most of the country and the app never closes.
Same raccoon. New outfit. To win one hundred dollars on a typical bet you have to risk one hundred and ten.
Guess who wins that one.
No drive and no dress code. Just you and your phone in bed at two in the morning.
So here's what I wish someone told me before Friday. Not financial advice. Just the stuff the casino really doesn't want you to know.
One. Treat it like a concert ticket. Decide the price before you walk in and leave the cards in the hotel room.
Two. Bring your own clock. Set an alarm on your phone because the casino will never show you one.
Three. When you win walk away. I know. Revolutionary.
And four. If it stops being fun talk to someone. In the US you can call one eight hundred gambler any time.
So I walked out with the two hundred dollars I had left and I called it the price of a very loud show.
The casino waving goodbye to me.
The good news is I learned how casinos really work. The bad news is it cost me three hundred dollars.
And remember the one trick I promised you at the start? It's this. They don't need you to lose tonight. They need you to come back.
So can you beat a casino?
No.
But next time I find out why insurance companies pay out billions every year and still make a fortune and I'm pretty sure I've been paying for it.
Subscribe so I can keep losing money for science. Unlike roulette the odds here are actually in your favor.
